en: The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on the Avaivartika-cakra, Volume One, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Yuezhi during the Western Jin Dynasty. Chapter One: The Dharma-Wheel of Non-Retrogression. Chapter One: The Dharma-Wheel of Non-Retrogression. The Buddha addressed the assembly: "In the past, immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless eons ago, there was a Buddha named Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, and Buddha Bhagavān. At that time, there was a king named Arciṣmanta who ruled over Jambudvīpa. He possessed great power and majesty, governed with righteousness, and his dominion extended throughout the four continents. His life span was eighty-four thousand years. At that time, the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū appeared in the world and turned the wheel of the Dharma for the first time. Having turned the wheel of the Dharma, he taught the Dharma extensively to sentient beings. At that time, King Arciṣmanta heard that the Tathāgata had appeared in the world and that he had turned the wheel of the Dharma for the first time. Hearing this, he rejoiced greatly and, together with his ministers, kinsmen, and retinue, went to the place where the Buddha was. Upon arriving, they bowed their heads at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times, and withdrew to sit to one side. At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the king’s thoughts, preached the Dharma extensively for him. After hearing the Buddha’s teaching, the king attained the stage of non-retrogression. Thereafter, the king established a great park for the Buddha and the Saṅgha, adorning it with various flowers, fruits, and fragrant waters. Within the park, he built a magnificent hall made of the seven precious substances. The hall was spacious and elegant, with pillars of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal. It was adorned with nets of pearls and jewels, and hung with banners and canopies of various colors. Within the hall, he prepared couches and seats, all exquisitely crafted. He also provided abundant offerings of food, drink, clothing, and bedding. When the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū arrived at the park, the king personally went out to meet him, bowed his head at the Buddha’s feet, and invited him to enter the hall. The Buddha accepted the invitation and entered the hall with the great assembly. Once seated, the king offered the finest foods and drinks, as well as robes and other necessities, all of which were of the highest quality. After the meal, the king took a low seat and sat to one side to listen to the Dharma. At that time, the Buddha preached the *Avaivartika-dharmacakra-sūtra* for the king and his retinue. Having heard this sūtra, the king and his ministers all attained the stage of non-retrogression. From then on, the king constantly practiced giving, upheld the precepts, cultivated patience, exerted vigor, practiced meditation, and cultivated wisdom. He also encouraged others to do the same. Because of these roots of goodness, after the passing of the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, the king was reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven, where he served Maitreya Bodhisattva. After Maitreya attains Buddhahood, the king will descend to be born in the human world and become a Cakravartin King, ruling over the four continents. He will then encounter the future Buddha Maitreya, hear the Dharma, and attain the stage of non-retrogression. This is called the first turning of the Dharma-wheel of non-retrogression. Thus spoke the Buddha. All the bhikṣus, bodhisattvas, and the great assembly, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and faithfully practiced it. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
At that time, during the final watch of the night, the World-Honored One arose from meditative absorption in the samādhi called Stainless Radiance.
The Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta likewise entered the samādhi of Universal Illumination, and the Bodhisattva Maitreya led the assembly of great beings into the samādhi of Universal Manifestation.
Thereupon, the worthy Śāriputra arose from his sleep in the latter part of the night; he left his own chamber and resolved to go visit Mañjuśrī.
As he was about to enter Mañjuśrī’s chamber, before he had yet entered, he saw the Buddha’s divine chamber and proceeded toward it.
He beheld one hundred thousand lotus flowers, beyond measure, surrounding the Buddha’s chamber; furthermore, he heard from afar the sounds of various kinds of great music.

Those great lotus flowers spontaneously radiated light, illuminating the Jeta Grove and pervading the entirety of Śrāvastī such that there was nowhere it did not reach; the splendor of the Buddha’s realm, the trichiliocosm, was magnificent and sublime.
At that time, Śāriputra immediately stood still and did not proceed; he checked himself and waited for Mañjuśrī, unaware that he had entered the latter’s chamber.
Standing before Mañjuśrī, he beheld him sitting cross-legged, serene and absorbed in meditative concentration.

At that time, Śāriputra snapped his fingers, yet [Mañjuśrī] never awoke; he uttered a loud voice, yet [Mañjuśrī] did not stir. Furthermore, with single-minded focus, he contemplated the great transformations manifested by Mañjuśrī, which were so profoundly moving.
He observed that his body was within the great ocean; struck with alarm, he desired to emerge from the chamber of Mañjuśrī’s samādhi, yet he could not withdraw at all.
He attempted to rise into the air by means of his supernormal powers, but he was likewise obstructed; though he exhausted all his spiritual faculties, he could not soar or fly.
Furthermore, he saw his own body, along with Mañjuśrī and their dwelling, spontaneously moving toward the east.
At that time, Śāriputra stood before Mañjuśrī, sat down in the full lotus posture, and gazed at him without weariness.

At that time, to the east, beyond as many buddha-lands as there are sands in the Ganges River, there was a world named Sound of Non-retrogression; the Buddha there was named Most Excellent Radiance of the Blossoming Lotus.

The worthy Śāriputra followed Mañjuśrī and beheld that Holy Honored One; from every one of his pores there issued forth lotus flowers, each of which was forty thousand *li* in circumference and illuminated the entire trichiliocosm of Buddha-fields.
Those lotuses number one hundred thousand; their stalks are made of exquisite jewels, and they possess lion thrones of diamond and purple-golden hue, upon which all the bodhisattvas sit.

They are non-retrogressive regarding the unsurpassed, right, and true path; having attained dhāraṇī and the five supernormal powers, they delight in the personal accomplishment of the dharma-patience (dharmanidhyāna-kṣānti), and their bodies are adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man.

The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Most Excellent Radiant Lotus-Blossoming was born amidst lotuses that were pure and flawless; their colors numbered in the hundreds of thousands beyond measure, with stems of blue beryl exquisitely interlaced, and seats made of the finest sandalwood and precious jewels, with extraordinary pearl bells suspended on all four sides.

That seat was empty and solitary; Mañjuśrī immediately took his place upon it, and together with his lotus lion-throne, he leaped upward to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, whereupon he returned at once to the Buddha.
He prostrated in salutation, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and returned to sit upon a lotus flower; before that World-Honored One, he joined his palms in self-refuge.
Then, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Most-Selected Radiant Lotus-Blossom questioned Mañjuśrī:
"O Benevolent One!..."
"Why have you come to this land in vain? Mañjuśrī replied,
"Indeed, World-Honored One!"
"I have come from the Sahā world.

At that time, the attendant of that Buddha—a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Gentle Voice and Soft Resonance, who was intent upon the unsurpassed, true, and correct path and had attained the stage of non-retrogression—adjusted his robes over the lotus throne, knelt with palms joined, and asked that Buddha:
"How far is that Sahā world from here?"
That Buddha said to him:
"To the west, beyond lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, lies the Sahā world; it is from that land that Mañjuśrī has come."
The Bodhisattva Mṛdusvaraghoṣa again asked the Buddha,
“What is the name of the Buddha in that world-system called Endurance?
Does he currently exist there?”
The World-Honored One replied:
"His name is Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; he is currently preaching the Dharma.
Again, they asked the Buddha:
"What kind of Dharma does that Great Sage Buddha manifest?
The Buddha said,
"He opens the way of the three teachings."
The attendant asked again, "What are these three? [The Buddha replied:
"The Śrāvaka, the Pratyekabuddha, and those who propagate the Buddha-way; such is the teaching of the Dharma by Śākyamuni Buddha—these are the three paths of the Dharma."
The attendant asked again:
"Do the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, differ in their preaching of the sutras and their transformative teachings?
The Buddha said:
"All are equal.
With a gentle and soft voice, he again asked the Buddha,
"What is meant by 'equal'?"
The World-Honored One replied:
"To discourse on non-retrogression—this is called equality.
He asked again:
"Why does the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Kāśyapa proclaim the teachings of the three vehicles? The Buddha replied:
"The people of that land are stubborn and difficult to transform; their minds are inferior and their wills weak, making it difficult to save and deliver them through the Single Vehicle alone."
For this reason, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, employ skillful means (upāya-kauśalya) to preach the Dharma.
The Tathāgata Śākyamuni has arisen in an age of the five turbidities; by means of these skillful means, he delivers beings according to the principles of the times.
He asked again: "Indeed, World-Honored One!
Is the difficulty of the diligent labor involved in teaching and transforming beings in that Saha world truly like this?"
The Buddha said, "It is indeed so;
there is diligent toil and perilous suffering.
The attendant asked again:
“We are truly fortunate and have gained great benefit, O World-Honored One, that we were not born in that land.
The Buddha said, “Cease this; do not speak such words.”
"You ought to abandon them and reform yourself, repenting of your transgressions.
He asked again:
"For what reason should one reform the past and cultivate the future?"
"Furthermore, it is extremely difficult to preach the Dharma in the Sahā world; for this reason, we do not wish to go to that land.
The World-Honored One replied, "Virtuous ones, do not harbor such thoughts. Do not repeat these words; you must correct yourselves."

Why is this? Cultivating the roots of all virtues for twenty billion nayutas of hundreds of thousands of kalpas in this buddha-field is not equal to teaching the Dharma of the Perfection of Deliverance to people in the Sahā world from dawn until mealtime—thereby enlightening the ignorant and deluded, leading them to take refuge in the Triple Gem, and causing them to receive the five precepts.

To explain the paths of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas is already extremely difficult for a bodhisattva mahāsattva; how much more so to instruct them to become śramaṇas, to abandon the secular world and draw near to the Way, to protect them with the Dharma, to exhort, assist, and guide them in the meaning of wholesome dharmas, or even to cause the Great Way to flourish and be established—this is a teaching that is difficult for a bodhisattva mahāsattva to attain.
"Why is this? Because the world of Endurance (Sahā-lokadhātu) is full of many hardships and calamities.
He asked again:
"What is the concern?
The World-Honored One replied:
"Gentle tones and soft resonance!"

Even if a worthy one were to live for hundreds of thousands of millions of nayutas of kalpas, hearing and receiving [the teachings] from countless Buddha-lands where lifespans are exceedingly long and beyond measure, they could not exhaustively enumerate the immeasurable evil dharmas—lust, anger, and delusion—contained within this Sahā world-system.

Now, as I speak with my own mouth, I have explained the causes and conditions of that person's transgressions and blessings; furthermore, through the Buddha’s wisdom, I have clearly distinguished them. Yet, the defilements and impurities of that world of endurance (*sahā-lokadhātu*) are not yet exhausted and cannot be fully concluded.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Gentle Voice and Soft Resonance raised his voice three times and uttered this eulogy:
"How marvelous is the Tathāgata, the Able One!
Most compassionate Lion, King among Men!"
His virtue is lofty and sublime, free from all obstructions; he contemplates the World-Honored One with clarity and profound reverence.

By virtue of his original merit and his aspirational vows, he endures toil and maintains humility to expound the meaning of the Way for the sake of sentient beings. He eliminates the immeasurable fetters of lust, anger, and delusion, and instructs them to give rise to the minds of *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*, gradually transforming and enlightening them so that they may attain the state of a Buddha-Sage.
"Because they manifest the profound wisdom of the Way for the sake of all beings, they roam among the roots of all virtues, their resolve free from any hope for worldly glory.
Then the bodhisattvas took seven-jeweled flowers—resplendent in color, numbering in the hundreds of thousands, pure and free of dust.

Furthermore, there were immeasurable lotus petals born from diamond stalks; the lotuses upon which they grew were like dewdrops, composed of exquisite sandalwood and various jewels, adorned with distributed necklaces as their ornamentation. Their minds were enlightened and their vision clear through the fundamental virtues of their past lives; manifesting sublime and holy conduct through the transformations they had aroused, they appeared like magical illusions. With joyful and exuberant intent, they leapt into the void, holding these flowers in their hands. They turned toward the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Śākyamuni, and with single-minded devotion scattered the flowers across that Sahā world-system. Like a rain of precious canopies, silken streamers, banners, and pennants, they maintained their resolve to make offerings to the Tathāgata Śākyamuni.

Having scattered various incenses and burned sandalwood, blended perfumes, and powdered incense, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground in that land, bowed his head toward the west, and at that moment offered this praise:
"Homage to the Buddha Śākyamuni, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, and to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas of that Realm of Endurance!"
Clad in the armor of boundless virtue, they are resolved upon diligence; their minds are free from arrogance or indulgence, and their virtues are lofty and complete.
Their hearts are ultimately most honored, sublime, and sacred, as they revere the True Dharma.
Taking the Dharma as their strength, they felt compassion for all sentient beings and radiated great light, harmonizing with the practice of the One Vehicle.
With one voice and in unison, they all exclaimed:
"We wish to behold the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Śākyamuni and all the Bodhisattvas, so that the Buddha’s teachings and instructions may never be interrupted."

Then, the Tathāgata Most Selected Radiant Lotus-Blossom heard the sounds of the bodhisattvas’ songs and verses; examining the source of their minds, he expounded the Buddha-dharma for those bodhisattva mahāsattvas, analyzing its essential meanings so that their hearts were filled with joy.
He addressed the bodhisattvas, saying:
"O sons of noble family!

Would you not rather behold the place where the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One, and the bodhisattva-disciples of the Sahā world dwell? There they cultivate the teachings of that Buddha to transform sentient beings in accordance with their needs, desiring to deliver them from peril and distress, their minds filled with compassion."
Regarding the profound and subtle Dharma, they have never felt fear nor considered it difficult;
they have never slandered it, but have planted many roots of virtue.
Their minds are free from attachment and they do not hope for or seek reward, as they uphold the practice of the six perfections.

When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is born into a world of endurance, they honor the original vows of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, uphold the True Dharma, take the Way as their strength, and awaken to the conduct of all Buddhas.
The Bodhisattva replied:
“Indeed, World-Honored One!
Having received the Buddha’s holy instruction, I have seen it all.”
Furthermore, regarding the compassionate grace of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present, there shall forever be no net of doubt.
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Most Exquisite Radiant Lotus-Blossoming-Openness addressed the Bodhisattva Gentle-Voice-Sound:
“You all should go together with Mañjuśrī to the Sahā world, where you shall respectfully practice his instructions so that your minds become radiant and clear.”
The Bodhisattva Mṛdusvaraghoṣa addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:
“We wish to go to the Tathāgata Śākyamuni to behold the Sahā world, so that by receiving your noble wisdom we may bring our vows to fruition.”
Mañjuśrī replied: "How wonderful it is that you practice thus!
O sons of noble family!"
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are difficult to see and difficult to encounter.
Why is this? Because they appear only once in hundreds of millions of eons.
We should all together with one voice offer worship and serve them.

For this reason, they appear in the worlds of the ten directions out of compassion for sentient beings, transforming them into entry into the Great Way and causing them to attain awakened wisdom. We should serve and comply with all classes of beings—those that crawl, those that breathe, and all other forms of life—and practice ritual reverence toward the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, inquiring about the scriptures so that the people of the ten directions may achieve supreme blessings.
The Bodhisattva replied:

"May our bodies be together with the Venerable One, so that we may pay homage to and receive instruction from the various Buddhas, and practice the noble wisdom to compassionately transform all beings."
Thereupon, Mañjuśrī bowed his head in prostration before that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, the Most Excellent Radiance of the Blossoming Lotus, and circumambulated him three times.

Together with the various bodhisattvas, who paid their respects with solemn reverence, and Śāriputra—who, having heard the Buddha’s teaching and received his instruction, gazed upon the Buddha without weariness and perceived the five aggregates of the body as being like an illusion—each offered flowers, incense, sandalwood, blended perfumes, powdered incense, silken banners, and streamers to make offerings to the Buddha. Having been inspired by the Buddha’s fundamental virtues, their minds became firm and resolute; they honored the Triple Gem and, desiring to deliver sentient beings, attended upon the Buddha.

As soon as he had finished speaking these words, in the time it takes to extend one's arm, he suddenly vanished and arrived before the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, in lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the eastern direction.
There, he listened to all those Buddhas expound this Mahāyāna sūtra, which is the non-retrogressive, Vaipulya, stainless, pure, and luminous teaching.

In all those buddha-fields there are no women, nor is there the teaching of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; the virtues and meanings of all those buddha-fields are entirely equal and pure, just like the buddha-field of the Tathāgata Most-Selected Radiant Lotus-Blossom, being identical without distinction.
The Bodhisattva’s place of enlightenment filled the Buddha-fields, and from the navels of all those World-Honored Ones, lotus flowers emerged identically.

Mañjuśrī, manifesting transformations upon his seat that were universal, maintained a uniform dignified demeanor as he made offerings to the Buddhas—those in the east, south, west, north, southeast, southwest, northwest, northeast, above, and below. At that time, throughout the lands of the Buddhas in the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, Mañjuśrī appeared before them all, pervading everywhere without exception.
All those Tathāgatas fully expounded this faultless Vaipulya Sūtra of the Non-retrogressive Wheel.
All their attendants were reverent and solemn, setting their minds upon the Great Way; kneeling for a long time with palms joined upon lotus flowers, they asked their respective Buddhas:
"For what reason has the Tathāgata Śākyamuni established these teachings of the three paths?"
They all desired to go to the Tathāgata Śākyamuni to inquire about and receive his Dharma teachings, seeking his grace and salvation through Mañjuśrī.
They also addressed the bodhisattvas of the ten directions, saying:
"You should attend upon Mañjuśrī and together proceed to the Buddha-land of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni."

Then, while the night was not yet light in Jambudvīpa within this Sahā world-system, the venerable Ānanda saw a radiance entering through the window of the veranda; he immediately rose from his bed, intending to leave the vihāra.
Beholding the Jetavana, its radiance was like that of day; looking up into the void, he did not even see the moon.
Examining the Jeta Grove, he saw only water—azure as jade, supple and clear—with no trees or dwellings visible at all.
He thought to himself:
"This morning I am to expound the Great Profound Dharma; for this reason, these auspicious omens have first appeared.
At that time, Ānanda lifted his foot and entered the water; the water did not cling to his feet, nor did he become wet or submerged, and he was filled with great joy.

He went to the divine chamber desiring to see the World-Honored One. There he saw ten million lotus flowers surrounding the Buddha’s chamber, and he also heard a magnificent sound accompanied by various musical performances.
Light emanated from the lotus flowers, illuminating the Jeta Grove and the city of Śrāvastī; throughout the trichiliocosm, there was nowhere it did not reach with its brilliance.
With a heart full of joy and anticipation, he bared his right shoulder, knelt with palms joined, prostrated in salutation, and took refuge in the Buddha.
As the morning star appeared and the night drew toward dawn, the great lotuses that had been surrounding the Buddha’s chamber entered the Jeta Grove and settled in their midst.
Ānanda thought to himself:
"Now it is fitting that I go to provide a seat for the Buddha; this shall be an auspicious omen for the foundation of his preaching of the Dharma.

As soon as he had finished arranging the seat, the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system shook in six ways. The same occurred in each of the Buddha-fields of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of ten Ganges Rivers. This great significance was fully realized by all, who were without exception struck with wonder and joy.
Blue lotuses, red lotuses, yellow lotuses, and white lotuses pervade the Buddha-field; trees grow spontaneously, their branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits likewise flourishing in abundance.

The assembly of bhikṣus each wished to leave their dwellings but were unable to do so on their own; they saw that the Jeta Grove was submerged by water, yet the water was soft and clear, and as they stood at the doors of the vihāras, they beheld only a great radiance.
Each thought to themselves:
"Today the Great and Subtle Dharma shall be preached; for this reason, he has first manifested these miraculous responses.
At that time, the World-Honored One, the Great Sage Śākyamuni, arose from samādhi, emerged from his divine chamber, and proceeded to the lion throne.

As soon as the Buddha’s body was seated, at that very moment, the bodies of all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, in all worlds throughout the ten directions, emitted a great radiance; the various colors were each distinct and beyond measure, such that there were none among those common people who did not behold them.
Thereupon, Mañjuśrī traveled throughout the ten directions, accompanied by a multitude of bodhisattvas, visiting all buddha-fields and making universal offerings everywhere.

This great bodhisattva led the assembly of mahāsattvas, manifesting inconceivable supernatural powers to rescue and benefit sentient beings; upholding and conforming to the Buddha-dharma, he taught and liberated them, guiding them according to their various inclinations, and having thus finished preaching the Dharma for the people of the ten directions.

Mañjuśrī saw the Tathāgata Śākyamuni seated upon the lion throne, and all the bodhisattvas together emerged from the earth within the Jeta Grove; accompanied by immeasurable billions of hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of bodhisattvas, they circumambulated the World-Honored Buddha innumerable times.

Each manifested an incalculable number of lotus flowers with one hundred thousand petals, each of a different color, as an offering to the Buddha; these lotuses were spread throughout the Buddha’s realm without any gaps.

Furthermore, this bodhisattva scatters sandalwood incense, blended incense, powdered incense, and exquisite incense; the fragrance of these completely permeates the trichiliocosm, causing beautiful fragrances to arise everywhere.

The fragrance of generosity, observance of precepts, patience, diligence, single-minded concentration, wisdom, and the supernormal powers of skillful means; the flowing fragrance of the Dharma; the subtle fragrance of the bodhisattva’s path-wisdom of the six perfections; and the fragrance of practicing the realization of the meaning of the sutras—these various fragrances all radiate a great light.

2. Chapter on Upholding Faith, from the *Anavatapta-nirdeśa-sūtra*, Chapter Two: Upholding Faith. Thereupon, when the World-Honored One had spoken these verses, the Venerable Ānanda stepped forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"For what reason does the Most Victorious One further sustain those of firm faith until they reach the stage of Pratyekabuddha?"
“Does the Tathāgata manifest only the Dharma of the bodhisattvas? He replied, “It is so.”
Ānanda, you should know that it is only the thorough exposition of the Bodhisattva sūtras that is supreme. Why is this?
Because I have personally arisen in this world of five turbidities, where those who are indolent and negligent harbor weak and inferior aspirations.

If the will attains entry into pliancy, tranquility, and serenity, there is nothing further to be contrived; suffering and pleasure are eliminated.
Inducement has no source from which it arises; there is neither arising nor ceasing. This is the peace of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), gradually leading toward great wisdom and omniscience.

"For what reason has the Tathāgata preached this extraordinary sūtra?

Countless billions of devas, nāgas, and spirits were all filled with hesitation, wondering:

"Countless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of bodhisattvas did not understand why the World-Honored One praised and extolled the bodhisattva path, yet spoke of faith, the four fruits of the śrāvaka, and the pratyekabuddhas."

"Why is this? Because this Dharma is so subtle and difficult to understand, for this reason the Tathāgata remains silent and speaks not.

"What is meant by 'knowing that words are merely sounds'?

With reverent composure toward the Buddha, with a mind ultimately pure and bright,
and always being steadfast in the Path and the Dharma— this is called upholding faith.
Far removed from the six afflictions, with a mind that seeks nothing,
and having eternally eliminated the five aggregates— this is called upholding faith.
If there are those who do not yet accord with the Way, one should exhort and transform them so that they may find joy.
To have no doubt regarding the Buddha-dharma is what is called upholding faith.
If one sees those who rejoice, and encourages them toward the resolve for the Way,
yet does not seek to grasp at the mind within oneself, this is what is called upholding faith.
Wisdom is equal toward the six sense-fields; the dharma-realm is without distinction or exception.
Within the lands there is nothing to be gained; "lands" are but words and sounds for the ear.
The mind constantly contemplates the beginning and the end; like space, it is devoid of self.
Possessing great power in wisdom— this is called upholding faith.
Delighting in practicing the noble precepts, pure and without negligence,
Perfectly endowed with both morality and concentration— this is called upholding faith.
Delighting in the realm of profound stillness, sentient beings are likewise so;
that they possess the ultimate characteristic is what is called upholding faith.
Not abandoning any person, the dharma-realm is also thus.
If one were to calculate the species of those sentient beings, the number of worlds would be inconceivable.
Just as the dharma-realm is without distinction, such faith is what constitutes ultimate understanding;
therefore, one praises steadfast faith, for the bodhisattva has nothing to fear.
Sentient beings are all spontaneous; when reckoned, they have no place of abiding.
Universally understanding that phenomena are empty, that state cannot be apprehended.
All people are unconditioned, and those multitudes are likewise empty.
This is the tranquil nirvāṇa; therefore, it is revealed to all.
If a bodhisattva is courageous and understands sentient beings in this way, they shall receive a name and be praised as one who upholds faith.
When one's practice of the Dharma is thus profound, it is praised as "upholding faith.
Ānanda! You should uphold this; you should likewise explain it with discernment.

"Ānanda! On this account, I have followed the path of practice without remainder; through this Dharma, I have attained equal enlightenment, and the Bodhisattva has manifested this radiance. Thus it is, Ānanda!"
For this reason, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha praises and establishes the bodhisattva as one who upholds faith;
considering this meaning, he guides them through skillful means.
Chapter Three: Honoring the Dharma. From the *Anavatapta-nirdeśa-sūtra*, Chapter Three: Honoring the Dharma. The Buddha addressed Ānanda:
"For what reason does the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, praise and extol the Bodhisattva’s honoring and upholding of the Dharma?"
The bodhisattva abides herein in the Buddha-way without regressing.
Grasping the tracks of awakening, they discern them with clarity, never transgressing the dharma-realm.

Attaining inconceivable mastery of the scriptures, they maintain total retention (*dhāraṇī*) while constantly remaining unmoving; their will conforms to the words of the Dharma as they examine all doubts.

All dharmas are naturally devoid of any attachment; that which is upheld through total retention (dhāraṇī) has no basis or establishment. In accordance with total retention, one does not cling to the literal text of the sūtras.
One whose will always delights in the holy and reveres those who seek the Way has no grasping toward any dharma; it is by practicing non-grasping that one expounds the Dharma.

"His will and nature are benevolent and harmonious; his movements and halts are peaceful and secure. He preaches the Sūtra of Quiescence, upholding this Dharma herein without clinging or abandoning it.

All that is spontaneous is the mark of the Noble Path; having attained this meaning, he never transgresses or loses what his person practices. His essence remains constantly firm and abiding, for the world is not a place of existence."
"What is meant by a bodhisattva constantly observing?

It means never perceiving this body as dwelling in stability or tranquility; naturally conforming to the True Dharma, they remain equanimous within the objective realm, neither departing nor arriving."

Having formed this understanding, one realizes that the Dharma taught by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas has resulted in the attainment of these scriptures, which are pure and stainless; one perceives that all phenomena are neither joined nor dispersed.
"When all the sūtras suddenly cease to appear, one does not see the unconditioned nature (*asaṃskṛta*) of all phenomena.
Because they are not seen, there is nothing upon which to rely; since no phenomenon is seen, there is nothing to be grasped."
Knowing that the realms are like empty space, one then expounds the scriptures; all conceptualizations naturally cease, there is no frivolity, and it is formless and cool.
"To be free from mind and without mind, such that the mind cannot be apprehended—if it cannot be apprehended, that is the mind of the Way."
Yet, without coming or going, they preach the practice of tranquility; they do not engage in verbal discourse and have no longing or seeking.
Regarding the Dharma in this way, being without dependence or cause, they do not rely upon it nor give rise to the appearance of dharmas.
Constantly following the sūtras is the dharma of a bodhisattva; yet, being without attachment, they do not give rise to [the notion of] nirvāṇa.

That which he explains is like making something manifest: one does not long for lineage to obtain such a state, but rather abandons all lineages to attain the bodhisattva practice of the dharma of non-attainment.

"In all comings and goings, there is neither going nor coming; in all wisdoms, there is no past, future, or present. To maintain faith in this way—unwavering, unshakable, non-retrogressive, and non-abandoning—and to uphold all dharmas with neither haste nor laxity: this is called upholding the Dharma and attaining the Bodhisattva path."
Having attained the noble practice, there is nothing to be attained; it is by accomplishing such a state that one is called a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who "Honors the Dharma.
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
"The teachings of all Buddhas Have never known any regression."
To uphold the sutra in this manner is to uphold the Dharma.
To expound the Buddha-dharma of all Buddhas— beyond conceptualization,
not spontaneous, profoundly deep, and ungraspable— is to uphold the Dharma.
Never having disparaged the various realms, for the dharma-realm is inconceivable;
because one has attained that meaning, it is called "upholding the Dharma.
To serve the Dharma with earnest sincerity is the practice of all Buddhas.
When the mind has no attachments, it is called upholding the Dharma.
When there is no grasping at progress or regression, and all phenomena are seen as natural,
with no attachment to any of the various sutras, it is called upholding the Dharma.
Not abiding in quiescent extinction, one upholds and treads the Great Path;
by conforming to those scriptures, one is said to "uphold the Dharma.
The Way is eternally the Dharmakāya; thus one yearns for and seeks the subtle and wondrous teaching.
To cast aside indolence is to uphold the Dharma.
To listen to the sutras and receive them, to study, contemplate, and practice them repeatedly;
to be benevolent by nature and dwell in peace—this is to uphold the Dharma.
Constantly expounding the meaning of serenity, holding the sutras without attachment,
and attaining the practice of non-conceptualization— this is what it means to uphold the Dharma.
With a steadfast mind established in the Way, one practices with clear wisdom and without dwelling.
Always being without a body within the body—such is their profound understanding.
Reaching the state of the empty body, the dharma-realm is thus equal;
there is neither going nor coming, for they have eliminated all conceptualizations of the body.
Whatever teachings the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have expounded, to universally attain this sutra is to be a holder of the Dharma.
All dharmas are unconditioned; that realm is exceedingly pure.
To offer this sutra in this way is to uphold the Dharma.
To extensively examine all sutras and see them as they appear and yet not see them—
if one does not perceive any phenomena, then there is nothing to be upheld.
All these realms are empty; thus one expounds the Dharma-realm.
Naturally free from all conceptualizations, it is formless and without frivolity.
The mind relinquishes all existence, and even its intent cannot be apprehended.
Even if one cannot attain the mind, this mindfulness is supreme.
When the will is free from conceptualization, one expounds the Dharma according to the meaning of tranquility;
being without words and without attachment, this mind is truly honored.
Because one can honor this Dharma, That which is aroused is free from attachment;
Not relying upon any realms, This is what constitutes upholding the Dharma.
The Dharma honored by Bodhisattvas Should accord with the scriptures in this way.
Not relying on that which cannot be raised up, he manifests the absence of any agent.
Practicing such virtuous training, he accords with those various lineages;
because he has attained this meaning, he praises and extols the lineage.
Because one plants [roots] within this lineage, it is called the meaning of a bodhisattva;
one who can accord with this dhāraṇī is one who upholds the Dharma.
Fully not perceiving any phenomena, there is nowhere for anything to go.
Even if they were all to rush toward it, it would still not be that dharma.
In the future, there will be no destination; one who understands all dharmas and fully comprehends the *dhāraṇī* is neither restrained nor shaken.
Without abandoning, there is nothing to pursue; that is the dharma of creative construction.
Without elevating, there is nothing to lower; one who holds the dhāraṇī delights in the Dharma.
Regarding all phenomena as non-phenomena, one preaches without attachment.
Not to seek within the various sutras—this is what it means to uphold the Dharma. Ānanda!
For this reason, I have expounded the bodhisattva practices to bring about the attainment of the subtle and wondrous Way; this is what it means to praise all dharmas.
Ānanda! For this reason, I compose songs in praise of those who uphold the Dharma, for they conceive of the Way as profound; I guide such individuals as these.
These innumerable teachings have been bestowed, and are praised by the Bodhisattvas.
"Because of skillful means and eternal peace, I therefore praise this sutra.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"For this reason, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, extols the bodhisattva’s dharma of dhāraṇī; the meaning manifested herein is likewise a skillful means."
Chapter Four: The Eightfold Equality, from the *Anavatapta-nirdeśa-sūtra*. The Buddha addressed Ānanda:
"For what reason does the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, extol the meaning of the eightfold equality of the bodhisattvas?"
In this regard, the bodhisattva remains far removed from the eightfold wrong paths and attains the gates of liberation without attachment.

Without relying on the eightfold right path, they transcend the dharmas of ordinary beings, establish themselves in the meaning of the Way, and attain the central truth. Surpassing the mundane, they vow to establish themselves in the wisdom of the Way; seeing no path to be gained, they emerge from deviant tracks and abide constantly in right contemplation, attaining the trace of equanimity.
Detaching from the body of craving, may you abide in the meaning of the Path and attain the Buddha-body.
Abandoning the notion of a personal self, constantly contemplate the Buddha’s teaching, and maintain an impartial mind toward all beings.
"Stay far removed from the attachments of sentient beings, always dwelling in non-reliance, and sever all dharmas.
Why is this? Because dharmas cannot be grasped; they are the power venerated by the body."
Detaching from worldly registers, one admires the scriptures that transcend the world;
one attains the fixed realm of reality (*dharmadhātu*).

Neither failing to reach the Way and its teachings, nor remaining detached from the mundane, one explains the meaning of existence and non-existence, and reverently cultivates the level and even path.
Abandoning thoughts of attachment, one perceives no distinction between the mental states of the past, future, and present, yet does not grasp at the notion of attaining the Way. Why is this?
Because when one’s resolve is equal toward all and one cultivates universal wisdom, neither poisonous fire nor swords and staves can endanger the body.

"Having completely relinquished all realms, they reach the Buddha-lands; without departing from the various paths, they establish themselves where there is no coming or going. Wherever the Path comes and goes, they always propagate great peace; therefore it is said that the Bodhisattva’s path has no abiding."
Why is this so? Because the Buddha-way is empty, it has no location.
Since there is nowhere to abide, the blade does not turn toward the body, and none can cause harm; this is what is called attaining peace.
Having now reached this state, there is neither that which has been learned nor that which has not been learned, nor is there anything further to be sought.
Not having attained the status of a sage or noble one, my will has never aspired toward such things.
For this reason, the blade cannot harm me, and my body cannot be shaken.
All paths follow emptiness; by discerning the wisdom of emptiness, one cannot be harmed by weapons.
By employing great compassion, one attains the realm of tranquility among sentient beings and reaches the realm of serenity.
Vast giving is not mere pity; it abandons anger and hatred.
One who practices loving-kindness illuminates brilliant wisdom, transforms the world through compassion, and achieves great pity (*mahākaruṇā*).
Not dwelling in the realm of persons, his compassion is fully perfected; even a blade cannot wound him.
He is equal to the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm; he is equal to the dharma-realm and the realm of equanimity, for in the Way there is no diversity.
Without giving rise to conscious thoughts, free from anger and resentment, and detached from frivolous play, one remains tranquil and silent.
Such is the nature of the Dharma-realm; transcending all that exists, the Bodhisattva performs deeds with single-minded devotion.
Wherever all sounds reach, the Dharma has nothing to which it may be attached, nor does it abide in beginning or end.
The inclinations of the multitude are merely sounds; as for those who clearly understand and expound the transformative Dharma, they speak with the conceptualization of existence and non-existence.
By abandoning the notion of self, one transcends all sounds and voices, surpasses both equality and heterodoxy, and attains this teaching.
One understands that all phenomena are merely words and sounds; yet, not even a single phenomenon is apprehended, for there is no one who crosses over.
This is called the eightfold equanimity;
one never yearns for or becomes attached to any sounds.
Thereupon, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"By abiding in the eightfold equanimity, one attains the eight gates of liberation;
being unattached to these eight, this is called the eightfold equanimity.
Transcending the eight practices of ordinary worldlings, one comes to abide in right discernment."
Not perceiving any intermediate wisdom— this is called the Eightfold Equanimity.
Transcending the conduct of worldly folk and attaining abiding in the Buddha-way,
therein there is nothing to be acquired— this is called the Eightfold Equanimity.
Distant from all false views, one cultivates right view;
attaining the path of equanimity, this is called the Eightfold Path.
By removing attachment to self, one establishes the true and holy Way.
Attaining the body of a Buddha— this is called the eightfold equality.
Abandoning the notion of sentient beings, constantly resolving to cultivate the conduct of a Buddha,
and treating self and others with impartiality— this is called the eightfold equality.
Having transcended the notion of sentient beings, one dwells in the placeless;
when all phenomena have utterly passed away, this is called the Eightfold Equanimity.
Abandoning worldly dharmas, one reverently practices the noble and correct teaching.
To bring about the meaning of profound stillness is called the Eightfold Equanimity.
That which is abandoned is the conventional dharma; the Buddha-way is likewise so.
To have no attainment regarding this dharma is called the Eightfold Equanimity.
To speak of there being but one essence, and no duality of extremes—cleansing away such notions is called the Eightfold Equanimity.
Not dwelling in the middle, and having no intention to sever or cling in practice; this is the path.
The wisdom of the Path is like a level plain; this is called the Eightfold Equanimity.
Not apprehending the mind of the past, and likewise regarding the future, remaining level and even in the present—this is called the Eightfold Equanimity.
At first there is no mind from which it arises; as for one who gives rise to the thought of the Way, this mind cannot be apprehended. By what cause does such a one attain the Way?
By entering into non-attachment; like the Sage, there is nothing that can be apprehended.
For this reason, neither sword nor poison can harm him.
Having escaped the five realms of existence and the source of manifold marks, he is fully perfected in his coming and going; therefore, he is called the Deceitless One.
The Way is relinquishment and not worldly involvement; it is merely sounds and voices.
By casting off all attachment to echoes, one does not deceive oneself.
One cannot find its origin, for it has always been thus.
Coming and going consist only of the body of sound; it is merely to exhort the learner.
Because peaceful transformation exists, there are words; yet that peace is likewise empty.
By training in accordance with this, one is able not to deceive oneself.
The Bodhisattva’s practice and cultivation consist in fully mastering such wisdom;
that nothing whatsoever is severed is what is called not deceiving oneself.
He does not covet himself, even if there were a sharp blade.
One cannot inflict harm upon such a person; there is no one who can cause them to waver.
Universally compassionate toward all beings, delighting in the Way with great pity, they have cast away the mind of malice and injury;
even a sharp blade cannot prevail against them.
Should there be those who wish to harm you, realize that your own body is empty and non-existent;
thus you shall attain the Way of the Buddha—how then could a blade cause you injury?
Having reached the state of profound stillness, you cast off all evil paths.
All calamities are utterly extinguished; the edge of the blade cannot cause harm.
Having accomplished clear wisdom, the noble one attains nothing lacking;
manifesting brilliance and reaching the Buddha-way, for this reason the blade does not harm him.
The realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm constitute the three realms;
being equal to these three realms, one does not deceive oneself.
When the seeds are equal, perfect enlightenment is attained; no distinction in names is perceived.
If there are no aggregates, what is there to purify? Purity lies in being far removed from frivolous play.
Entering this track of equanimity, one is therefore called a bodhisattva;
those who cling to sounds and voices will not escape the five realms of existence.
Although it is said that one reaches the ultimate dharma-realm, it is taught that there is nowhere to go;
by attaining the patience of non-abiding, this is called the eightfold equality.
Distinguishing the various echoes of sound, one expounds the dharma of profound stillness.
Non-conceptualization is not a name; therefore it is called the Eightfold Equality.
Having eliminated and released all sounds, one attains the realm of soundlessness;
by not clinging to any resonance, this is called the Eightfold Equality.
Through sound one understands all phenomena; all phenomena are of their own nature.
All phenomena have no names, and no one is seen who attains deliverance. Ānanda!
"Because I am thus, I praise the Eightfold Right Path; though its meaning resounds and leads toward this, there is likewise nothing to be attained.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha extols the Bodhisattva’s proclamation of the sound of the Eightfold Path; this discourse concerns the direction of skillful means and expedient wisdom."
Chapter Five: The Path of the Tracks. In the *Anavatapta-nirdeśa-sūtra*, Chapter Five, "The Path of the Tracks," the Buddha again addressed Ānanda:
"For what reason does the Tathāgata extol the bodhisattva as the path of the tracks?"
The path flows through to the Buddha-mind; when a bodhisattva abides herein, all that they initiate and create is forever without establishment.
Without advancing and without slackening, they transcend all dharmas and reach the flow of the Buddha.
They do not cling to benevolent wisdom nor rely upon dharmas; their practice is without attachment and they have no fixed abode.

"Endowed with wondrous conduct, they attain the traces of the sages; the vigor of these bodhisattvas is firm and strong, their minds compassionate and patient, never indolent; they cast aside arrogance and laziness to yearn for and seek the wondrous Way."
The world honors the supreme, yet one does not cling to noble conduct, nor does one dwell anywhere.
"To abide in this path while seeking all dharmas, that which is sought can never be obtained; it has never wavered."
Although they abide in the Path, they contemplate the birth and death of the sages; with the Buddha’s wisdom being impartial, they renounce all worldly pleasures.
They treat the aggregates and hindrances as equal, extinguishing all attachment to the body and false views, and diligently cultivate the contemplation of the Buddha.
"To examine that diligence and behold the noble path, completely eliminating all conceptualizations and transcending the notion of self—this is called the track of the Way.
Not clinging to the Buddha-path, one attains unconditioned awakening;
one does not doubt the sagely wisdom or the Buddha’s precepts."
Not relying on the world and not observing its precepts, through this state of non-seeing, one has no further seeking.
Without longing for precepts and having abandoned the three fetters, one abides correctly within the triple world and thereby attains great peace.
“Maintaining the thought of protecting all sentient beings, without attachment or defilement, and relinquishing all clinging, one attains the Buddha-way and reaches the state of tranquility.
Without reckoning one’s own body or life, one gives away all that one possesses without regret.”
The faculties are always joyful, and the expression of anger is cast aside.
One follows and cultivates the noble conduct; though bestowing gifts with generosity, there is no sense of relinquishment, for one rescues sentient beings from their straits.
Having already brought about deliverance, one does not abide in non-action.
Transcending all conceptualizations, one gives rise to the dharma of non-thought; casting aside the notion of a person, one attains this wisdom.
“Without fear of the assembly, he discourses on cessation.
By purifying the Buddha-way, he transcends all hardships and does not dread birth and death. Why is this so?
Attaining the tranquil Dharma free from blemish or defilement, the sublime transformation of the Sage brings wondrous peace.
Knowing there is no coming or going, one weeds out the various conceptualizations of the multitudes, abiding only in the clarity of the Right Path and the purity of resolute conduct.
Then the Buddha spoke in verse:
"I discourse upon that track of the Path; The Buddha’s sagely state is inconceivable.
If one calculates that among the multitude there are those who abide, Then one is being sustained by the Path."
The noble wisdom is the supreme peace; it does not rely on the net of manifold perceptions.
Being empty and quiescent, it abides nowhere; therein, nothing can be apprehended.
One who has attained this path is a bodhisattva of firm and resolute will.
Only those who follow this holy teaching find the World-Honored One unsurpassed.
Resolving upon the Way without greed, their minds constantly gather great wisdom;
taking this as the track of the Path, they do not rely on anything and remain unattached.
What is called the perception of birth and death, the Buddha-mind is likewise;
possessing perfect and impartiality, this is called understanding the path.
Free from the various aggregates and hindrances, one expounds and analyzes the dharmas of the path.
Therefore, having eliminated all [defilements], one realizes this as the track of the Way.
Sentient beings all rely upon the body; yet by giving rise to the mind to contemplate the Buddha-way, that which their will examines allows them to constantly behold the path of the Sage.
In the past, when my body first gave rise to fetters, I harbored the dangerous notion of a self;
because of this, there was no dust-free state, and I did not adhere to the Buddha-way.
At first, my mind was filled with doubt, wondering if I would not attain Buddhahood.
To resolve these doubts, one stands correctly in the Buddha-way.
If one understands the precepts and the prohibitions taught by the Buddha,
one eliminates all conceptualizations of "precepts," such that there is neither compliance nor non-compliance with the prohibitions.
Transcending the three fetters and abiding equanimously within the triple world,
one then attains the Buddha-way and discerns the perceptions of sentient beings.
Practicing the path of clarity through emptiness, one aspires for and seeks great wisdom.
Having attained the will for holy stillness, one does not cling to the Buddha-way.
Always practicing giving with a mind of equanimity, one casts aside expressions of anger;
thus there is no [grasping at] life, and one abides in the Way without negligence.
Never being arrogant or resentful, one rescues others from all afflictions and distress;
therefore, this is called the path of the tracks, abiding upon the higher road.
Never giving rise to various conceptualizations, one should practice non-attachment.
Having done this, one is no longer afraid; one wanders freely without prohibitions or precepts.
If one studies the various scriptures and, through skillful means, abandons all seeking;
and if one awakens to the realization that all sounds are mere echoes, then dwelling in the world, one has nothing to fear.
Even when attending assemblies, one encounters no difficulties;
thus, one proclaims the dharma of profound stillness and purifies the noble path.
When acting in the world, one gives rise to the perception of a person, thereby understanding spontaneous conduct.
Because one employs non-attachment, one then abandons all fears and difficulties.
If one abandons all calamities and harms, one will not fear the beginning or the end;
having attained the pure and serene Way, one is free from defilement and dwells in the supreme peace.
Having waited out the cessation of the evil realms, one thereby has nothing to fear;
this is the path of the supreme sages, wherein the grace of the Way is never absent.
This is the Dharma of the Bodhisattvas, manifesting the deeds of the traces of the Way.
For the sake of those who are indolent, negligent, or inferior, he speaks in order to guide and benefit them.
By means of subtle and skillful expedients, he expounds the holy path of the Buddha;
if one enters the state of a bodhisattva, that person has already become a leader.
The Dharma taught by the Teacher is always in accord with skillful means;
his fundamental practice was likewise so, as he aspired to the Buddha-way.
For this reason, Ānanda!
He analyzes and explains the path of the sages, yet the ignorant are as obstructed as if their will were blocked;
though they seek such [truth] with many thoughts, they cannot understand what is taught.
The foolish and deluded remain in darkness, slandering wisdom and diligence, even as they listen to these profound and essential aspirations.
Ānanda! For this reason, I praise the path of practice (mārga). Were there no bodhisattvas who have attained realization, only those [of the śrāvaka vehicle] would be able to understand it.
Through hundreds of thousands of countless scriptures, they are instructed and transformed in the path of practice.
"The sounds of treading upon the tracks manifest the illumination of the Buddha-way.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"That which the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha calls the 'radiance of the bodhisattva' as the track of the Way—know that this meaning is a skillful means (upāya-kauśalya)."
Chapter Six: On Coming and Going. In the *Avaivartacakra Sūtra*, Chapter Six: On Coming and Going, the Buddha again addressed Ānanda:
“For what reason does the Tathāgata extensively explain that a bodhisattva is one who comes and goes?”
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva enters the inconceivable wisdom of the Buddha-way, aspiring to seek the immeasurable causes and conditions of noble enlightenment.

Amidst all worldly clamor, he does nothing to create further entanglements; even when reaching the Great Way, his wisdom severs all conditions as he yearns for and seeks the illumination of the Buddha.
Seeking undisturbed dhyāna, transcending all concentrations, and shedding all defilements, one then attains the Dharma.
Equal to the Buddha’s scriptures and comprehending all sutras, one seeks only this meaning—the illumination of the path of virtue protected by the Tathāgata.
When a person has never moved and remains without transition, they are the Dharma-realm.

Out of compassionate concern for sentient beings whose minds are closed and whose intentions are obstructed—who encounter manifold sufferings and afflictions and do not understand the scriptures—one aspires to the Buddha-way and establishes them in this wisdom.
Yet his resolve was set upon the Great Illumination, the faculties and powers, the factors of enlightenment, the gates of liberation, and meditative attainments; he analyzed these meanings, thinking:
"How may I transform and guide all beings, causing them to aspire to the Buddha-way?"
"Always use this clarity to exhort and transform those at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), seeking the Buddha-eye with a mind free from the five hindrances (*āvaraṇa*).
If one enters right contemplation to guide and benefit the world, the wisdom for which one aspires shall surpass that of all the sages."

That wisdom which does not grasp at anything is the illumination that all dharmas ultimately converge upon, which cannot be apprehended; by means of this sagely state, one does not seek after sentient beings, yet spontaneously establishes them.

"In this regard, these various wisdoms realize that phenomena have no location; therefore, when beholding the realm of sentient beings in the future, they seek the unsurpassed state and aspire to non-thought, yet do not grasp that realm."
Neither coming nor going, they bring sentient beings to fulfillment; though they go, they do not go.

They transform and enlighten the people, understanding the abode of the masses, and they distinguish these meanings according to their transformation. Beholding these dharmas, one sees that all sentient beings abide within the Dharma-realm.
To examine through non-seeing and to govern the Dharma-realm with equanimity is to comprehend all things.

One views the Great Way through the level and evenness of the scriptures; by means of the Buddha’s sagely wisdom, one realizes that there is no person who does not understand the Way of humans, seeking such a state.
"The wisdom that is without grasping is free from defilement and dust; therefore, this wisdom has no improper locus.
To seek the path of great illumination through a wisdom that lacks [this] wisdom is to be unable to aspire toward the noble; this is the wisdom within wisdom, the wisdom of great illumination."
To have no seeking and for that seeking to have nothing to which it aspires—this is called the wisdom of noble clarity.
When a bodhisattva’s practice is able to attain this, their coming to seek [it] is therefore called "coming and going" (saṃsāra).
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"This wisdom involves coming and going; The Buddha’s insight is inconceivable.
Therefore, it is called 'coming and going,' As one aspires to seek the Buddha-way."
Through many causes and conditions, one opens the way to transformation; thus the path to Buddhahood is accomplished.
In this matter, wisdom is applied with equanimity, and through longing and seeking, there is no turning back.
Without relying on any meditative absorptions, one exhorts and transforms all amidst the dust of the world.
Wishing to rescue and deliver these beings, he is fully accomplished in coming and going.
Through the Buddha’s sūtras and the Dharma of equality, he discerns that persons lack marks;
understanding them as originally non-existent, he is thus said to come and go.
Regarding the Dharma that can be attained, one realizes all-encompassing wisdom;
I too shall attain this, seeking the place wherein to abide.
Without ever stirring sentient beings, nor calculating the various realms of phenomena, I seek my dwelling.
Therefore, regarding coming and going, one does not dwell near the place of rebirth.
With compassion for countless people who, possessing little wisdom, have encountered suffering,
and wishing to establish them in this wisdom, one seeks the Great Way of the Buddha.
The faculties, powers, and factors of enlightenment; Reciting and contemplating the three gates of liberation and dhyāna— Having analyzed these meanings, they seek the noble path of the Buddhas.
Aspiring to the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), They rely upon what the Buddhas of the past have relied upon.
Therefore it is called "coming and going," establishing the existence of the Great Sage.
One who yearns for and delights in the eye of compassion possesses the inconceivable Buddha-eye;
thus, through this coming and going, one yearns for the Great Way of the Buddha.
The noble quest of all Buddhas, the subtle and wondrous meaning of the World-Honored One—
having personally resolved upon this profound wisdom, it is the supreme state of omniscience.
It is that which is realized by clear insight and the ultimate refuge of all phenomena.
That wisdom cannot be apprehended, nor can the seeker of the Way.
He delivers countless beings and establishes them in supreme wisdom;
for this reason, there is coming and going, and those who come have something to seek.
Entering and beholding the realm of Buddhas, The realm of humans is inconceivable;
Thus, through coming and going, One rescues sentient beings therein.
Examining the realm of sentient beings, It cannot be found when sought.
Therefore, one should regard coming and going as a longing for the dharma-realm.
When the multitudes of beings have no destination, nor do they reach any realm of persons;
if one clearly understands those states, one will accord with the distinctions of their wanderings.
Beholding all phenomena, they see that these do not manifest;
always with a concentrated and settled mind, they seek the Great Holy Path of the Buddha.
Such subtle and wondrous wisdom is stainless and pure.
Yet the object of discernment is clarified, and that wisdom cannot be grasped.
That which the Bodhisattvas delight in is the transformation of sentient beings;
thus they attain that brilliant wisdom—by what cause have they come to this?
For this reason, Ānanda,
I discourse on coming and going for the sake of those of little wisdom, so as to reveal to them the thoughts that have arisen.
For this reason, Ānanda, I do so.

Chapter Seven: On the Non-Returner.
The Buddha again addressed Ānanda:
"For what reason does the Tathāgata describe the Bodhisattva Maitreya as a non-returner?"

Thereupon, the Bodhisattva, having transcended all existences through every practice he maintains and performs in all places, attains the Buddha’s illumination and eliminates all conditioned formations; having subdued these, he shall no longer return.
Why is this? Because one perceives that all phenomena have no coming or going.
Having transcended ordinary beings and relinquished worldly wisdom, one enters the Buddha’s clear and wise insight, attains non-abiding, and realizes that all phenomena are level and even.
Why is this? Because by attaining the realm of tranquility, one is no longer a wavering ordinary person; not establishing oneself in the noble path, one blocks all evil ways.
Strive to deliver yourself from emotional desires; regarding food, be without attachment to food, and reach the supreme traces of illumination.
Having uprooted all views, one is free from attachment; there are no longer any of the sixty-two false views.
Having transcended birth and death, one contemplates *nirvāṇa*; having surpassed it, one enters the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and relinquishes all conceptualizations.
They do not follow scriptures to pursue purity or defilement within the evil realms; they cast aside arrogance and harbor no self-conceit.

They emerge before the onset of ignorance and affliction, shatter craving and desire, extinguish all darkness, and uproot the pursuit of sensual pleasure. They set aside worldly dust, pride, and self-indulgence, bringing these hindrances to rest and distancing themselves from mundane wisdom; thus, through intentional reflection on the Buddha-vehicle, they equally attain noble insight.
When a bodhisattva renounces their will and abandons the realm of desire, they cultivate the primordial purity and the resolve for the noble cessation of the past.

Their wisdom is unsurpassed and is that which all Buddhas have realized; wishing to manifest this contemplation, it is the most honored and infinite among all sentient beings, serving as the vehicle for all—this is the wisdom of the Buddha.
When a bodhisattva attains these perceptions and non-perceptions, they equally eliminate the realm of all doubt; having reached this state, the bodhisattva no longer regresses.

Being far removed from all conceptualizations, all people are no different from emptiness.

Emptiness and the absence of emptiness are free from all conceptualization.
Through non-thought one reaches the Way, which eliminates [the grasping of] sentient beings.
The perception of space involves neither discarding nor non-discarding.
Why is this? Because all phenomena are fundamentally equanimous and pure, and there is nothing whatsoever among all sentient beings that is to be abandoned.
Because it is equal to that which is explained, there is nothing to be attained;
since there is no longer anything to be acquired, one does not come back.

"Regarding the conditioned and the unconditioned, he has fully awakened to the convergence of all phenomena and transcended all afflictions;

Because they have attained that which neither comes nor goes, this is called "no returning.

Regarding the practices seen by the multitude, there are sixty-two distinctions.
Not falling into that limit is called "non-returning. This dharma has neither end nor beginning;
having already abandoned all fears, this wisdom is as if originally non-existent; therefore, it does not arrive here.
That which is to be attained is unconditioned tranquility; not clinging to any worldly defilements, one passes beyond all manifold conceptions. For this reason, he does not come here.
Having severed all evil paths and washed away all stains and attachments, he has transcended them.
One who studies profound stillness and non-action is said to no longer return.
Having subdued the evil Māra, along with his retinue and weapons, he is forever free from manifold thoughts; for this reason, he does not come here.
He uproots delusion, sorrow, and grief; he eliminates the root of craving and desire, and severs the height of lust. For this reason, he does not come here.
Having subdued all defilements and eradicated manifold conceptualizations, [he remains].
Having attained ultimate, supreme wisdom, he is therefore called one who does not return.
Having cast off all sorrows and griefs, having destroyed arrogance,
and having brought about the cessation of the five aggregates, he is therefore called one who does not return.
The vehicle of resolve attains radiance; the Buddha-vehicle is unsurpassed.
Not craving the afflictions of desire, it is therefore called "no returning.
Having known the location of the Buddha-treasury, the foremost among all treasuries,
That which was expounded by the Buddhas of the past—therefore I do not go there.
That place belongs to the Honored Vehicle; the Buddha’s sagehood is unsurpassed.
Having severed all doubts—therefore I do not go there.
Having received thousands of countless people and exhorted them to establish themselves in the Buddha-way,
and because they have established themselves in the noble path, for this reason he does not come here.
He clearly understands the realm of emptiness and maintains an equanimous mind toward the realm of sentient beings.
Having distanced oneself from all notions of attachment, one therefore does not go there.
Understanding all realms clearly, the dharma-realm is likewise so;
since sentient beings cannot be apprehended, one therefore does not go there.
Distinguishing the realms of sentient beings, yet space is devoid of thought;
all phenomena are thus, and for this reason one does not approach them.
That person is without a [discursive] mind, having withdrawn and eliminated all conceptualizations.
When various thoughts do not give rise to the path, one is called a non-returner (*anāgāmin*).
For this reason, Ānanda, I praise and speak of the non-returner: all matters never return, and one abides in the Buddha-way.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

Chapter 8: On Non-Attachment. In the *Anavatapta-nirdeśa-sūtra*, Chapter Eight, "On Non-Attachment," the Buddha again addressed Ānanda:
"What is meant by the Tathāgata praising the bodhisattva as being 'unattached'?"
This bodhisattva has extinguished all conditioned activities and is detached from lands;
they do not rely on the Buddhas to liberate sentient beings;
they do not engage in the defilements of worldly toil nor in suffering and pleasure. Because they rescue all beings by extinguishing form and desire, they are called "unattached."
Not perceiving sentient beings and not grasping at the dust of desire, one does not crave suchness; therefore, it is called "non-attachment.
Having cast off all deception and dwelling nowhere, one realizes that all phenomena are empty; through this understanding of tranquility, one does not cultivate manifold conceptualizations.
When all perceptions are stabilized through meditative concentration, one eliminates manifold thoughts.
Without calculating that there is a person who destroys or extinguishes their aspirations, one realizes the emptiness of phenomena through wisdom and attains non-attachment.
The Buddha-way is free from discursive thought; being fully perfected yet relying on nothing, it is therefore called "non-attachment."
He expounds the scriptures to destroy all flaws, praising the teachings of the Perfectly Enlightened Ones of the past, while remaining heedful regarding those of the future and the present.
Being pure and free from defilement, one discusses only the state of profound stillness; therefore, this is called "non-attachment.
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas transform and instruct all people, establishing them in the Buddha-way and seeking the path of the sages, they harbor no longing for any phenomena.
Fully endowed with a mind of loving-kindness, he practices the benevolence of a Buddha, never dwelling anywhere.
Because his loving-kindness is such as this, it is called "non-attachment.
He transforms and establishes sentient beings yet does not perceive a person; having ultimately realized great compassion, he understands non-dwelling, and thus it is called "non-attachment."
For the sake of sentient beings, he bestows grace and perceives the Path; regarding phenomena, he has no conception of phenomena.
Having severed such [conceptions], he is called "Unattached.
He extols the power of awakening, reckons the number of vows, and attains non-abiding.

Knowing how to uproot the various roots [of affliction], they resolve to transform sentient beings; having realized the pure Dharma so as to fulfill the meaning of the Path, they never rely on anything, and thus it is called "non-attachment."
Beholding that which is not a place of reliance, one restrains greed for the body; regarding all phenomena, there is nothing upon which to rely or seek.

Furthermore, when in the midst of an assembly, one does not disparage any phenomenon, but preaches conditioned dharmas as being thus without a fundamental basis; therefore, this is called "non-attachment."
"Roaming through the lands of all Buddhas, they go without reaching anywhere; they do not give rise to notions of beginning or end, yet behold the Buddha, the Holy Honored One.

In the stage of non-retrogression, there are no women; one abandons the intent of the slumber of worldly afflictions.
One attains the sacred realm of the Buddha and the soil free from the hindrances of the aggregates, subduing the hosts of Māra and eliminating all enemies.
Entering the land of profound stillness, he manifests transformations that move all beings; he establishes himself in the lands of his vows within the realms sought by the multitudes.

The Bodhisattva, endowed with majestic brilliance, dwells in non-abiding; beholding and attaining the Buddha’s intent, he is sealed by the pure seal and brings peace to many lands. Having cast off all necklaces, jeweled ornaments, and the blemishes of defilement, he exhaustively realizes the stage of the unconditioned, the most supreme of all.
Having attained such a subtle and wondrous state of Buddhahood, all phenomena are empty; because one is fully endowed with the practice of the Path, this is called "non-attachment.
Having eliminated all worldly pleasures and rendered the sense faculties inoperative, one harbors neither hatred nor anger toward any phenomenon.
The vehicle of tranquil equanimity is the wisdom of the Buddha; body, speech, and mind alike practice supreme tranquility.
One who aspires to the noble path does not cling to tracks or traces, nor does one harbor thoughts of persons.

With compassionate mindfulness toward sentient beings—neither possessing a mind nor lacking a mind—he exhorted and transformed countless billions of people, establishing them in the Great Way and revealing it to all living creatures; he caused them to contemplate the Buddha-dharma and other such matters, guiding and benefiting the multitudes of common folk, leading them to give rise to the noble intention that is peerless.
All dharmas are uniformly empty and distinct; their fundamental emptiness and wisdom are established as identical, free from conceptualization.

Being able to know them thus with equanimity and without dependence, and having realized this, one should preach the Dharma to sentient beings according to their needs, without craving for various gains, without relying on scriptures, and fully possessing detachment from the sense bases.

To preach the Dharma in this manner is to be forever without words; though one brings about great transformation and salvation, one does not perceive oneself as delivering others, yet rescues all sentient beings.
One abandons all attachments and severances, frees oneself from craving for the body, and transcends all arrogance.
Beholding all phenomena as neither arising nor ceasing, one transforms the conceptualizations of sentient beings and the myriad things.
By not allowing form, sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness to be destroyed, the ordinary person remains unmoved and thus attains liberation.
To establish the Buddha-dharma and manifest the traces of the Path, one transforms others without partiality, thereby achieving the removal of hindrances.
Guiding and benefiting those upon whom they rely, one causes them to be free from the notion of a "Buddha," thereby providing diligent salvation and encouraging the arousal of the bodhisattva mind.

"Extensively cultivating the mind of non-attachment, one rescues others through the causes and conditions of the Way; putting an end to all turbid and distracted thoughts, one leaves behind delusion, madness, and deceit.

Fully endowed with samādhi and accomplishing the concentrated mind, one harbors no manifold conceptions, uproots perverse wisdom, causes others to behold right insight, and transforms and inspires the śrāvakas."

For those who aspire to turn back from their transgressions, he establishes them in reliance upon parents, wives and children, houses, brothers, and sisters, so as to cause them to eliminate affectionate attachment;
and he delivers them from attachment to lands, wealth, beauty, and the myriad things, as well as from the delusions of craving, the toil of worldly desires, and inverted views.
They transform and enlighten those who harbor attachments to the perception of myriad phenomena; they cause them to long for detachment from their homes and cultivate the silent will;

they cause those who are indolent, negligent, weak, or inferior to be liberated from all marks, thereby enabling them to enter the Buddha-land and fulfill the dharmas that purify desire and defilement.
"To arouse the aspiration for the Way with a mind free from duality, never giving rise to discursive thoughts—this is the unconditioned Dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).

To transform these classes of beings and give rise to the two marks [of male and female], one causes them to be without conceptual thought and to transcend all fundamental roots; therefore, it is called "non-attachment.
Whether among the World-Honored Ones and the worthy sages, or the indolent and the diligent;
whether men or women, the dull-witted and ignorant, or the wise and sagacious.

They clarify the sages and dispel the fetters; they guide and benefit these beings, causing them to be free from dualistic thoughts and leading sentient beings toward liberation. Therefore, they are called "unattached.

These bodhisattvas, whether their path is near or far, distinguish this meaning without giving rise to dualistic thoughts.
