Understanding emptiness and having no dependence, the Buddha-way is immeasurable;
through exhorting oneself to great diligence, one is thus called "Unattached.
Regarding the causes and conditions for preaching the sutras, one remains tranquil and free from frivolity.
Exhorting others to establish themselves in the Way and its Virtue, and bestowing upon them the name "Unattached" (Aśvaghoṣa).
The True Person practices loving-kindness, desiring to bring peace to all sentient beings;
because he exhorts others yet remains ungraspable, he is therefore named "Unattached."
Originally there were no sutras or scriptures; he bestows grace upon all classes of sentient beings.
Never having entertained the notion of a "person," he is therefore called "Unattached" (Asaṅga).
Having awakened to the power of the roots of true reality, he explains and analyzes it for the sake of others.
Having attained this wisdom within oneself, one is therefore called "Unattached.
Knowing the tranquil concentration of others and the path reached through the pure Dharma, one expounds the great teaching of the Sage; therefore, one is called "Unattached."
Not believing in the myriad things seen before one’s eyes,
that all are empty and non-existent— this is called being unattached.
Without relying on any Buddha-lands, yet practicing benevolence and righteousness within the realm.
The Abode of the Equal Enlightenment One, where he expounds the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings;
the True Person’s awakening to the Right Teaching allows him to perceive that which is non-perceptible.
To contemplate the Sage’s Awakening as it truly is—this is called being "unattached."
I have now realized the attainment of the natural realm;
it is ultimately without beginning or end—this is called non-attachment.
Having eliminated all objects of cognition, the mind harbors no anger or malice.
One should accord with True Suchness (tathatā) without resentment, practicing until the path of tranquility is perfected.
With a concentrated mind that does not cease, remaining serene and unmoving, one’s mindfulness of the Path is likewise; therefore, this is called non-attachment.
The person does not stir nor increase; the realm of sentient beings is likewise so.
Even the myriad sprouts are universally thus, as they are established through the transformation of the meaning of the Way.
Sentient beings and the Way—wherever they abide, there is forever no conceptual thought.
When calculation and wisdom are both entirely equalized, this is called non-attachment.
Being equanimous and without conceptual likeness, all phenomena are likewise so;
when the mind is upright as the Path, it is therefore said to be free from discursive thought.
One who is called an Arhat does not cling to any phenomena;
they are able to analyze and explain them for others, remaining tranquil and without dependence.
When expounding the meaning of the Dharma for others, though they speak, there is no teaching [as a conceptual entity].
Universally delivering immeasurable beings, he remains unmoved when beholding the multitudes.
Since no sentient being can be apprehended, he causes all people to sever their attachments;

Though moving and turning, one does not regress; though creating, one does not act.
Desiring to draw near to the Path of the Sages, one gives rise to this thought within the mind.
Having attained the Great Way, there is neither arising nor cessation;
though the mind constantly harbors thoughts and attachments, one seeks through them the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Toward those who receive existence as sentient beings, the benevolent person extends compassion to all living creatures.
For this reason, he is called "Unattached," rescuing and delivering all who harbor conceptual thoughts.

named 'Abiding in Non-attachment,' one attains the unsurpassed path.

Chapter Nine: The Disciples (Śrāvaka-varga) In the *Avaivartika-cakra-sūtra*, Chapter Nine: The Disciples, the Buddha addressed Ānanda:
“For what reason does the Tathāgata illuminate the bodhisattvas as being [like] disciples?”
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva transforms and edifies countless, incalculable people, causing them to hear the Buddha-dharma and discern the scriptures; therefore, they are called Śrāvakas.
He causes them to listen to the Noble Path and to purify themselves through non-negligence; therefore, they are called Śrāvakas.
They cause others to hear of non-action, peace, and the ambrosia;
the faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, foundations of mindfulness, and right abandonments.
By being fully endowed with these matters, they swiftly reach the wisdom of the Path; therefore, they are called Śrāvakas.
"It causes them to attain the wisdom of emptiness, whereby the body is found to lack solidity; yet those who are ignorant remain closed off and do not understand.
Why is this? It is because they are greedily attached to the various sense-bases of their own bodies."
The eye exists for the sake of forms; when one contemplates them in this way, one attains the Buddha-eye, whose vision universally perceives the inconceivable.
The eye has no dependence; by bringing this eye to ultimate perfection, one reaches all dharmas, and is therefore called a śrāvaka.
"Consider all these dharmas to be like an echo; do not become attached to their sounds.
There is no speaker, nor is there any listener;
there is no fragrance, no perception of fragrance, and no act of smelling."
For example, it is like a person who, while lying down and dreaming, smells various fragrances; yet upon waking, they realize these have no fragrance.
This is merely the product of conceptual thought. All fragrances smelled by people are like dreams, lacking any solidity.
Those who understand this sound are called śrāvakas.
"The tongue’s tasting of flavors is likewise empty.
If a piece of meat were to become the tongue, or if a wise person understands this, they would not be deluded by flavors.

Do not contemplate the six elements through the discrimination of flavors; then the mind will be opened and understood, and the intellect will not be negligent.

Chapter Ten: The Pratyekabuddha Chapter of the *Avaivartacakra Sūtra*. The Buddha addressed Ānanda:

It is that which has no form or likeness and cannot be destroyed; it is the present contemplation of phenomena that cannot be extinguished; therefore, it is called the Pratyekabuddha.
The scriptures of the Buddhas are inconceivable; they clearly understand that all sentient beings are entirely like *nirvāṇa*.
Having neither internal nor external, they cannot be grasped; all phenomena (*dharmas*) neither arise nor cease.

"The fundamental limit of persons is nirvāṇa; what is termed 'fundamental purity' is merely an attachment to words. Thus, the dharma of non-existence cannot be attained, for although names are proclaimed and spoken, they reach no destination."

"Examine for yourself that the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) is merely sound.

Neither arising nor ceasing, that which is spoken is spontaneous (*svabhāva*).
One does not cling to a self, nor can anything be found to endure for long; how much less so in the case of verbal expression?
When the eye perceives the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), there arises sensation (*vedanā*); when the aggregate of sensation ceases, it no longer has a name.

That which is called the aggregate of sensation is empty in its expression; it neither arises nor ceases.

"To understand the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) is to contemplate the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha);

"Regarding the matters of the five aggregates, one is forever without attachment to any of these; because one does not create the various causes, one is called a Pratyekabuddha.

Not clinging to any forms, ultimately there are no marks.

Sentient beings are intent upon the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and their minds cannot be grasped.

There is no arising and nothing to be extinguished, just as it is praised and chanted with the mouth.

Thereupon, the immeasurable hundreds of thousands of people who had gathered for the assembly heard these words and were all filled with doubt, asking:
"What does this mean? What is its intended significance?"
His mind was filled with profound despondency; if even an Arhat would utter such words, how much more so a worldling?
Those who were standing remained upright, and those who were sitting sat in silence, unable to rise.
The venerable Ānanda, having received the intent of the World-Honored One and fully knowing the thoughts in the minds of hundreds of thousands of countless beings, asked Mañjuśrī:
"Having heard the words of the Elder, all those gathered here are filled with doubt."
"I do not understand to what ultimate goal this discourse leads.
Furthermore, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, remains silent and says nothing. Mañjuśrī then said:
"O benevolent Ānanda!

This sutra is titled 'The Ground of the Bodhisattva’s Wheel of Non-retrogression. It is that which the elders and others may expound, and it is to be witnessed with the eyes and heard with faith by all non-retrogressive bodhisattva-mahāsattvas."
Ānanda asked again:
"Venerable sir, for what reason do you say this?
The World-Honored One remains silent."
"Are these elders [destined] for unsurpassed, perfect, true, and non-retrogressive [enlightenment]?
He replied, "Indeed;
they shall attain perfect awakening and shall never again turn back."
Mañjuśrī said to the Venerable Ānanda:
"The practice of lack of wisdom is called their mother.
These people have utterly eliminated all that is beneficial; they harbor no virtuous thoughts and are greedily attached to sensual pleasures."
This constitutes being a father: eliminating unwholesome perceptions, distancing oneself from all emotional attachments, and reaching the state of non-attachment.
One abandons the dharmas of ordinary worldlings, washes away impure conceptions by distinguishing the sacred from the profane, and shatters manifold thoughts without destroying the Great Dharma;
one gives rise to the intention of the Tathāgata to eliminate all conceptualizations, such that among all dharmas, nothing arises.
Therefore, the Elder spoke these words:
"Today we are fully possessed of the five heinous crimes.
Why is this so? Because a heinous crime involves no returning or going back.

Regarding what the Elder said concerning the accomplishment of the five pleasures: if one examines those five pleasures and finds them all to be like dreams, illusions, reflections, and mirages, and if one realizes this wisdom and acts without deficiency, that constitutes the five pleasures.
Why is this so? Because there is no fundamental basis; if its source is absent, it is completely eliminated.
Thus, one accords with equanimity and expounds the fullness of noble wisdom, thereby attaining the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*). This is called the fulfillment of the five joys.
"As for what the Elder has said—
'We have today become separated from right view and abide in wrong view'— he perceives all phenomena as being situated within wrong view."
How deceptive are all phenomena! They are false and illusory, yet appear as if they were true; in reality, they are utterly non-existent.
They are like empty space, devoid of form or appearance; whether empty or real, coming or going, they have no destination and cannot be grasped or preserved.
Why is this so? Because their origin is natural (*svabhāva*), and when one calculates these various dharmas, they are all equal and uniform.
Just as all dharmas are equal, so too is false view; it is not that these monks are unequal or free from falsehood.

Why is this? Because by departing from all conceptualizations, one attains the noble path of the Buddha, realizes the various factors of enlightenment, and becomes fully satisfied with the meaning of the sūtras, yet remains without anything to be acquired. Therefore, Ānanda!
All these bhikṣus spoke together, saying:
"Today we have fully embraced false views and abandoned right view. These elders are as follows:
"Today we have taken the lives of countless hundreds of thousands of people.
When these words were spoken, incalculable and countless tens of millions of humans and gods heard all dharmas.

It is like an illusion, a dream, a reflection, an echo, or a mirage; having eliminated the notion of a person, being without a self, and distancing oneself from the concept of a life-span, one transcends all roots of merit and gives rise to the mind of the Great Way.

Without planting any seeds, they shall give rise to the principle of practicing the Way, as will the other bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās, who renounce their lives for the sake of me and others.
With the perception of no-body, one no longer undergoes the afflictions of repeated births and deaths.

Why is this? Because the perceptions of self and person, as well as the perception of non-exhaustion, are forever exhausted without remainder; having attained the ultimate, one realizes the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Therefore, they spoke these words:
"Today we have slain the lives of countless hundreds of thousands of people. As for what those elders said:

"When we say, 'Today we have attained the Buddha-way and reached parinirvāṇa in the realm of no-remainder,' it means that we have transformed and enlightened the lives of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of people, causing them to cast off all defilements and attain the Noble Way."
Why is this? Because they have all resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, true, and correct path to enlightenment.
When these words were spoken, they all attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
For this reason, they sighed with admiration and praised themselves in verse, saying:

"Today our kindred have uprooted sensual desires and attained the Dharma of the Buddha-way; we are now free from the body of defilement and have removed all remaining impurities. Therefore, we say that we have now attained the Great Way and entered parinirvāṇa within the realm of no-remainder."
"These worthy ones, because they abide in the Mahāyāna, do not aspire to be among the devas.
O virtuous Ānanda!
When sons and daughters of good family resolve their minds upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path and engage in worldly affairs, their minds remain pure and are not bound by worldly dharmas."

One should then give rise to the mind that transcends all meanings; through the Path one abandons all conceptualizations and brings the sūtras to ultimate completion, thereby attaining parinirvāṇa within the realm of no-remainder.
This, Ānanda, is what it means.
Those who train in the Bodhisattva vehicle and practice the conduct of a Bodhisattva do not train in following the sun.
It is only the foolish and deluded who follow the recollection of the sun;
they are not people of wisdom. Why is this so?
If there were no such sincere faith to govern the celestial palaces, there would be no radiance, and thus no coming or going;
if the past were not obscured by darkness, there would be no day or night, and thus no mental reflection.
Foolish and ignorant people give rise to thoughts day and night;
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, in silent cultivation of the Great Way, associates with virtuous friends and possesses no lofty ambition or discursive thoughts of day or night.
"Why is this? Because by eternally eliminating all discursive thoughts, one attains the Buddha-way. Thereupon, Mañjuśrī spoke in verse:
"Regarding what is called 'not harboring [the thought of] giving': one cherishes oneself and calculates that there is a self;
if one does not sever this, it is said to be unshakable.
By discerning anger, the notion of it naturally does not arise."
The Noble Path, being without a fixed location, cannot be moved.
That which is called the "mother" is that from which all things arise in the beginning and end;
to uproot this root and bring it to nothingness is what is meant by "taking life."
Not following right mindfulness as one's father, one delights in the dharmas of sensual desire;
these are understood to be fundamentally non-existent, ultimately having no root.
To transform them so they return to the bodiless state, one does not know where the light proceeds.
Immovable and dwelling nowhere— this is what was previously taught.
The dharma practiced by Arhats, and likewise the dharmas of ordinary worldlings—
all those through which craving can be exhausted— this is what was previously taught.
Greatly giving rise to the perception of conditioned phenomena, one examines the self as being natural;
when all dharmas are free from attachment, there is no sound of speech.
This is what the Tathāgata knows, and what was contemplated in ancient times.
One who immediately uproots these very roots and stumps is said to be without source of birth.
By relinquishing such perceptions and attachments, one becomes equal and non-dual;
if one understands this, it is called the teaching of equality.
Regarding what are called the pleasures of the five desires, worldly people praise these five;
yet one should eliminate the notion of permanence and contemplate them as being like illusions and transformations.
When they are fully possessed without deficiency, one harbors no craving or desire for them.
For this reason, the World-Honored One praised those of such a kind before the assembly.
Discerning all sins and merits as being like a dream,
they understand through wisdom that ultimately nothing arises from anywhere.
Perceiving the phenomena of false anger as empty and quiescent, they cannot be solidified;
false views are but deceptions, while that discernment is sublime wisdom.
All phenomena are unreal; let none draw near to such dharmas.
Empty phenomena cannot be relied upon, for they are like space, having no location.
To perceive all things through universal understanding is why it is difficult to achieve right view;
this Dharma is level and even, and through clear wisdom one sees perfect equality.
Those who are ignorant and deluded give rise to the conception of a person, and thus they perish;
yet when one seeks the person and cannot find it, there is no one who dies.
When immeasurable people arise in birth, they then abandon the conception of a life-span.
Because he was free from the notion of a multitude, yet reckoned the transgression of a "life-principle" to be heavy;
having eliminated the perception of a sentient being and harbored no thought of a lasting life-span, for this reason he spoke these words: "I have slain countless people."
Having abandoned all the dust of afflictions, the Dharma is neither appropriate nor inappropriate;
understanding that the Way has no form or appearance, there is nothing to be destroyed or removed.
Having subdued the powers of Māra, one attains the pure Dharma of the Way.
"All dharmas are without contention; they neither arise nor cease.

When Mañjuśrī had spoken this verse, at that very moment, the minds of five thousand who harbored doubts were opened and their intentions were resolved; they attained great radiance and achieved the patient acceptance of the non-arising of all phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Each took his own robe to offer as a gift to Mañjuśrī, and at the same time they spoke these words:
"May we attain this Dharma-wisdom.
May we preach in such a manner as to transform and enlighten the masses, discerning profound wisdom without any obstruction, just like you, O Benevolent One."
Thereupon, the World-Honored One praised Mañjuśrī, saying:
“Excellent, excellent! This is most wondrous and supreme!”
"He has resolved all nets of doubt and drawn near to the sacred scriptures of the Buddha.
The worthy Ānanda stepped forward and addressed the Buddha, saying,
"What has Mañjuśrī taught and transformed, that the World-Honored One now praises him in such a manner?"
The World-Honored One then said:
“Mañjuśrī has guided and transformed countless hundreds of thousands of human beings, leading them to enter the Great Way, so that they have all fully understood the meaning of this profound sūtra.”
Ānanda replied, “Indeed, World-Honored One!
Are you preaching the wheel of non-retrogression for entry into the noble path?”
The Buddha said:
"It is so, Ānanda! One preaches the Great Way that transforms beings by means of the wheel of non-retrogression."
"Why is this? Mañjuśrī is a virtuous friend who guides and benefits all sentient beings.
Ānanda asked again:
“O God among Gods!

These bhikṣus standing before the Buddha all harbor thoughts of faithful adherence to and veneration of the Dharma, as well as the conceptions of the eightfold noble path, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, arhatship, and the states of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.”
“Can such as these give rise to the mind of the Great Way?
The World-Honored One replied, “These people are indolent and negligent;
their minds are weak, inferior, and clouded. Lacking a joyful and benevolent resolve, they are difficult to transform.”
"Proud and indolent, they fail to advance; their minds are set on food and clothing rather than practicing the profound Dharma, and they covet worldly gains from the Dharma.

They engage in conditioned activities and the distractions of turmoil, which provoke the eightfold equalities of confusion and violence; thus, they lack tranquility, and their faculties remain unsettled."
Their minds are negligent and they are arrogant and conceited.
They harbor notions of a self, a life-span, and a person; they do not abandon their manifold defects, violating the precepts and being greedy and envious.
Though they seek the Buddha-dharma, they follow entirely evil friends, delighting in false wisdom and refusing to accept it with reverence.
Though possessing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), they follow external conditions and crave the pleasures of wealth, beauty, food, and clothing.
From antiquity to the present, though rising early and sleeping late, they have not applied themselves with single-minded diligence, thereby violating the Way and its righteousness;
they engage in double-tongued speech, harsh words, lying, and frivolous chatter, harboring malice in their hearts and constantly quarreling with one another.
They place great weight on sin and merit, yet do not believe in the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
They seek to eliminate all conditioned practices through neither arising nor ceasing, and they destroy all dharmas so that no perception remains forever; this is what is meant by that.
Thereupon, the Buddha remained silent and did not utter a word in response.
The venerable Ānanda, receiving the Buddha’s majestic power, asked Mañjuśrī:
"For what reason does the World-Honored One remain silent and say nothing?"
Mañjuśrī replied: “In the final age of the five turbidities, such is the nature of people and the Dharma: they do not believe in the profound sutras; for this reason, the Buddha remains silent.”
Ānanda asked again:
"Is it possible that those who have faith all become faithless? He replied:
"Those who have faith are few indeed.
Ānanda, it is like this: those of clear wisdom are rare, while those who are ignorant and deluded are many. Why is this so?"
They do not delight in practicing, and for this reason they do not understand it.
Thus, Ānanda, those who hear this Dharma rarely have a sense of joy; for the most part, they do not find it pleasing.
Even if there are those who have faith, he is abandoned by the multitude and does not receive respect.
Whenever he enters a commandery, kingdom, district, town, village, or hamlet, people treat him with derisive laughter. Why is this so?
"Due to the influence of past offenses, they are shrouded by obscurations, and their original merit is meager.
Ānanda asked again:
"Regarding what was just explained, those who have little faith—what is the underlying meaning of this?"
Mañjuśrī replied, “Such individuals as these have abandoned the Buddha and do not believe in the Great Way.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha:
“Please expound it for us.
Though those who delight in it may be few, upon hearing what the Buddha has spoken, they shall all rejoice.
At that time, the World-Honored One surveyed the four quarters and then extended his tongue, covering the trichiliocosm.
From his tongue-organ, he emitted a great radiance that illuminated lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

At that time, the fourfold assembly, receiving the Buddha’s holy intent, beheld with their own eyes how the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, in lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the eastern direction, were all preaching this Dharma of the Non-Retrogressive Wheel; those present in this assembly all heard it from afar, without any difference.
When the assembly of the four classes of followers witnessed this transformation, they all became equal in mind and, with one voice and different mouths, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We only pray that the Great Sage will uphold and honor the wheel of non-retrogression which he has praised; it is exactly as the Buddha has spoken, and not otherwise."
"We have personally witnessed immeasurable and inconceivable Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, preaching this profound sutra with no difference whatsoever; it is only the Buddha who speaks it.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One withdrew his tongue and addressed Ānanda, saying:
"As for those who speak such falsehoods, may they never obtain a tongue such as this!"
Ānanda replied, “No, O God among Gods! It is because those who uphold the utmost sincerity,
who are transformed by the righteous Dharma, who accumulate merit, and who have followed [the path] through incalculable eons, have revealed great wisdom that they have reached this state.”
Therefore, O Holy One! You should indeed speak of it.

Should there be sons of noble family who possess faith and joy, even if their learning be meager and slight, once they have heard this teaching and beheld its clear evidence, they will immediately rejoice and practice it without ceasing.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"All four classes of followers who have not yet encountered this scripture shall set their minds upon its semblance.

When bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, gandharvas, kinnaras, and mahoragas hear this sūtra, they shall attain non-retrogression and reach the unsurpassed, perfect, true path of supreme, right enlightenment."
"And yet, in this land, he expounds the meaning of the Dharma without any difference from what I do now.

At that time, the fourfold assembly, as well as the devas, nāgas, and spirits, were filled with great joy; the net of their doubts was forever rent asunder. They all held flowers and incense in their hands and scattered them over the Buddha, while all the women lowered their precious necklaces of jewels and scattered them over the Buddha as well.
With one mind and equal intent, they all addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Today, the Great Sage, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, speaks without duality.
The Buddha again addressed Ānanda:
"It is truly as you have said; indeed, there is no difference.
What the Tathāgata has expounded is truly without dual speech, except for the removal of all defects and the greed born of ignorance."
"If one contemplates the Buddha, the God among Gods, with wisdom, then one shall obtain their wishes.
Ānanda asked the Buddha,
"What is meant by 'contemplating the Buddha with wisdom'?"
The World-Honored One asked him,
"Do you not understand this? He replied:
"I am not quick-witted.
How could I possibly reach such heights? O Benefactor of the Multitudes!"
He said: "If there were anyone who heard of the Buddha Śākyamuni, they would all become non-retrogressive on the noble path to buddhahood. Why is this? Because—"
The Buddha-way and universal wisdom are beneficial and cause no harm; they eliminate greed, hatred, and delusion—how much more so when one offers even a single flower to the Tathāgata?
After my parinirvāṇa, if you uphold the śarīra relics, make offerings to them, and take refuge in them, you shall all attain your heart's desires.
Ānanda asked again:
"If one practices with diligence and without doubt, listening to the sutras with single-minded devotion, will they all attain non-retrogression and become Buddhas?
The Buddha said:
"If there are those who hear of the Buddha Śākyamuni, they shall all attain unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. Why is this?
Were it otherwise, the Buddha’s word would be inconsistent, resulting in two contradictory statements."
The Buddha asked Ānanda:
"Suppose the shade of a *kūṭaja* tree covers five hundred chariots, and five hundred people are situated beneath it, all being sheltered by its canopy; how large would its seed be?"
He replied, “It is very small.
The Buddha said:
“Ānanda! Just as the kovidāra tree has a very small seed, yet when watered at the proper time it gradually grows large, spreading its branches and leaves to cover a vast distance;
how much more so for one who is devoted to the Buddha-way and hears the name of the Holy Honored One?”
One should likewise plant these roots of virtue and gradually cultivate their practice; being neither destroyed nor corrupt, they shall lead to the unsurpassed, right, and true path. Why is this so?
This source for planting the seeds of all dharmas is forever non-abiding.
Since sentient beings are fundamentally non-existent, there is no destruction;
the seeds of all dharmas are manifested without any dependence.
Ānanda asked the Buddha:
"Is it only the Buddha who speaks this as the holy original vow, or is such the natural way of the Dharma for all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones?
The Buddha said:
"I have made this vow: that all who hear my name shall never again regress and shall attain supreme perfect enlightenment;
such is the nature of the Dharma of all Buddhas. Why is this so? "
"The dharmas of all Buddhas are equal. Ānanda asked again:
"If they are indeed equal, what need is there for a vow?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas hear this sutra being preached, whether they have made a vow or not, they will inevitably attain realization upon hearing this Dharma."
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Never before has there been such a thing, World-Honored One!
This Dharma is subtle and wondrous; it is only through the Great Wisdom of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, that the multitudes are enlightened and transformed."
The Buddha said: “So it is, so it is, Ānanda!”
With great wisdom and vast illumination, he has transformed many and established them in the holy intent.
Within this Buddha-field, I have shown compassion toward all crawling and breathing creatures, not begrudging my own body or life;
I give away everything I possess without stinginess, practicing diligence without slackening, and remaining unattached to any phenomenon.
"By practicing the Bodhisattva path, accumulating merit and virtue, desiring to save sentient beings, and cultivating the profound scriptures, one shall attain the Way of the Buddha.
Ānanda asked the Buddha,
"It is difficult to fathom, World-Honored One!"
"Now that this sutra is being preached, will Mara not come to obstruct and disturb those who study it, preventing them from giving rise to virtue and setting forth upon the unsurpassed,
true, and correct path? The Buddha said, "Mara shall not hear of it."
"Why is this? It is because of the miraculous transformations of Mañjuśrī’s supernatural power.
Thereupon, Mañjuśrī immediately withdrew his majestic spiritual power.

At that time, Māra Pāpīyān, from afar in the void, heard the sound of the preaching of the Dharma-wheel of non-retrogression; hearing the words of the Dharma spoken by the Buddha Śākyamuni, his heart was filled with fear and his hair stood on end, as he spoke these words:
"Having surpassed me, they have used their power and might to empty my realm; there are no longer any territories remaining."
Filled with grief and weeping tears, he was so utterly aged and emaciated that he resembled a man of a hundred years, decrepit and senile.

At that time, Māra Pāpīyas transformed his body in this manner, and together with the fourfold army—comprising all the various Māras, their officials, subordinates, and classes of devas from throughout the trichiliocosm—they proceeded to where the Buddha was.
The military weapons were strictly arrayed, and the majesty of the hosts of Māras pressed upon the Bodhisattva.
When he first attained Buddhahood, he manifested an aged body, holding a staff and bearing the scars of battle, with a wrinkled face and sagging skin.
He stationed his fourfold army in the void, where they all together heard from afar the voice of the Tathāgata Acala, and their minds all attained meditative concentration.
Then Māra, realizing that he was no longer his own master, stood alone and solitary without any attendants; he went straight before the Buddha and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"Now I am but a single person with no attendants at all; I am emaciated and extremely old, with no one to support me."
Furthermore, lacking power and unable to overcome my own state, I find my realm empty and devoid of a kingdom.
The Tathāgata’s great compassion extends to all sentient beings; may He likewise take pity on me.
“World-Honored One!
My realm has been entirely emptied and forever transcended; there is no one left to support me or provide me with water and food.
The Buddha addressed Māra, saying:
“The species of sentient beings are exceedingly numerous and inconceivable.

Even if all Buddhas were to appear daily in numbers as vast as the sands of the Ganges, and each were to inspire immeasurable, incalculable billions of nayutas of classes of sentient beings, the species of sentient beings would never be exhausted.”
Māra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Indeed, World-Honored One!
Although the species of humans are many, I am now solitary and alone; I have no followers or servants, and there is no one to assist or support me.”
Suppose while practicing the Way, one suddenly becomes exhausted and falls to the ground, unable to rise by oneself; may they find comfort and attain joy and gladness.
We only pray that the World-Honored One will compassionately and swiftly nurture them, so that their kinsmen may flourish.
The Buddha said to Māra:
"Settle your mind for now.
Those who do not hear this Dharma and remain devoid of faith are all your companions."
Māra was immediately filled with joy and a wholesome mind arose within him; he spoke these words with his mind and his mouth:
"I shall transform people so that, even though they hear this Dharma, they will not believe or take delight in it."
"My mind harbors doubt and I am already hesitant; I must follow your teaching.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyān again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I only pray that you will extend your compassion and exercise great kindness, comforting me once more, so that I may leap for joy and be free from all sorrow and distress."
The Buddha previously taught:
"Upon hearing the name of Śākyamuni, all shall never regress and will surely attain the realization of the unsurpassed, true, and correct path.
We pray that the Holy One remain silent and do not proclaim this teaching.
When these multitudes of beings hear this, they will immediately apply themselves with diligence and establish themselves in the Great Way.
The Buddha replied to Māra, saying, “Settle your mind for now; do not harbor fear.”

I shall cause sentient beings not to establish the aspiration for the Way, but to remain within the human lineage; may each person find peace and remain unmoved, unshaken by form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
The Buddha shall guide them so that they do not remain apart from wrong views, nor establish right contemplation, nor harbor the sixty-two kinds of doubt;
all things are immovable, and they do not dwell upon the past, the future, or the present;
nor do they separate themselves from harming living beings, killing, stealing, lust, envy, false speech, double-tongued speech, harsh speech, frivolous speech, as well as jealousy, anger, and doubt.
Nor do they encourage others to enter the Right Path;
nor do they transform others through generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, single-minded concentration, and wisdom;

nor do they instruct others to practice the four debts of gratitude—bestowing gifts upon others, benefiting others with affection, benefiting all equally, and providing rescue and relief according to the proper measure.

Without relying on or being moved by anything, one does not conceive of the categories of people; one has no thoughts of parents, brothers, wives, children, or men and women; and one relinquishes all thoughts of movement regarding relatives and friends, days and nights, months, and half-months.
"Pāpīyān, rest assured.

I shall exhort people to eliminate thoughts of the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā), as well as the power of the mind set on the Great Way (mahāyāna-citta-bala), the powers of fearlessness and the faculties (vaiśāradya-indriya-bala), the factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga), and the practice of the Eightfold Path (aṣṭāṅgika-mārga). By transforming the masses through conceptions of the Buddha, the Dharma, the Noble Saṃgha, and the meaning of the path to omniscience (sarvajñatā), I shall cause them to remain unshakable within all phenomena."
At that time, Māra was so overcome with joy that he could not contain himself; his complexion immediately became radiant and his face shone with luster.
He scattered flowers over the Buddha, circumambulated him three times, and then spoke in verse:
“O World-Honored One, the Perfectly Awakened One, my heart was originally filled with exultation.”
"The words of the Perfectly Awakened One are never in vain; what he has undertaken shall surely be as he intends.

Having spoken this verse, Māra Pāpīyān immediately returned to his celestial palace, where he and his retinue indulged themselves in the five kinds of music, no longer feeling sorrow or concern for those who have resolved upon the Great Intention.
When the World-Honored One spoke this Chapter on Subduing Māra, the trichiliocosm shook in six ways.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Is it because of Māra’s majestic power that the earth is shaking so violently?”
The Buddha said,
“When this ‘Chapter on Subduing Māra’ was preached, sixty-four thousand people attained the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
Ānanda asked again:
"Is there anyone who still harbors doubt and has not attained full understanding?
The World-Honored One said, "Just now, upon seeing this, everyone was gripped by doubt and perplexity; each thought to himself:"
"I have heard this; what does this statement mean?
Where does it lead? Having said this, they did not see one another again.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha:
"I pray that the World-Honored One will swiftly manifest great radiance for this assembly to sever their web of doubt.
For it was for the sake of Māra that the Tathāgata spoke thus:"
“Pāpīyān, rest assured: I shall transform the multitudes so that they do not abide in the Way, yet they remain unmoved within the realm of sentient beings.

They shall not give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment nor possess dependent wisdom; they shall not abandon false views nor dwell in right contemplation; they shall not shift from their sixty-two doubts;
and they shall likewise have no notions of past, future, or present.”
It is not to abstain from killing, stealing, lust, false speech, frivolous talk, double-tongued speech, harsh words, as well as envy, anger, and doubt;
nor to cause others to fail in giving, precepts, patience, diligence, single-mindedness, and wisdom;
nor to be unfilial toward parents, siblings, wives, or children.
There is no day or night, nor month or fortnight; free from these manifold perceptions, one is likewise unmoving.

One causes [beings] not to fail in the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā), the fearlessnesses (vaiśāradya), the bases of power (bala), the factors of awakening (bodhyaṅga), the Buddha-dharmas, the noble Saṃgha, and all-knowledge (sarvajñatā), ensuring they do not waver.
